title: Carrot Girl
author: Catherine Baker
source: FFT Tutoring with the Lightning Squad (tutoring.fft.org.uk), screenshots supplied 6 Oct 2026

pages.heading: The Only Super
pages.text: It’s not easy being the only Super in a family of Normals. Of course, Mum, Dad and my sister Grace are good at loads of things. Mum is amazing at DIY, Dad can magic up a perfect chocolate cake, and Grace is a maths genius (compared to me, anyway). They don’t actually have superpowers, though.

pages.heading: Super Relatives
pages.text: Mum says my superpowers come from her side of the family. I’d never met my Aunt Bella, Uncle Mark and cousin Jake, because they’d been living in Australia till a couple of months ago. I’d certainly heard a lot about them, though. They all have really impressive superhero names, and superpowers to match. Aunt Bella is Splashwoman, and she can instantly knock over her enemies with a powerful jet of water. Uncle Mark is MarvoMind, and he can not only read other people’s thoughts but actually change them. Cousin Jake is Rocket Boy, and … well, you can probably guess what Rocket Boy can do.
pages.imageAlt: A cartoon of three superheroes running: a woman with flowing red hair, a boy in a red suit and cape, and a man in a blue suit.

pages.heading: Carrot Girl
pages.text: Unfortunately, my superhero name is Carrot Girl, and I have the sort of superpowers you might find in … a carrot. I don’t know if you know this, but some people think eating carrots can help you see in the dark. I’m not sure that’s actually true, but one of my carroty superpowers is that I can see quite well in pitch darkness. It comes in quite handy sometimes – for instance if I want to creep down to the kitchen for a midnight snack. However, it’s not exactly the kind of superpower you could use to defeat a supervillain.
pages.imageAlt: A girl with glowing blue eyes in the dark, resting her chin on her hand.

pages.heading: Danger Glow
pages.text: Oh – the other thing is that my skin glows an orangey colour when danger is near. I suppose that might be useful in theory, if I ever got anywhere near a dangerous situation. We live in boring Snoring on Sea, though, and I’m not even allowed to go into town on my own, so there’s never been much chance of that.
pages.imageAlt: Close-up of folded arms, with the skin glowing bright orange.

pages.heading: Do I Have To?
pages.text: As far as I was concerned, my superpowers were always a bit embarrassing. So, when Mum told me I had to go and stay with my Super relatives for summer holiday, I started to panic. There was no way I could compete with Rocket Boy and the rest of them! They were bound to think I was pathetic. “Do I have to, Mum?” I whined. “Yes, Emily!” said Mum firmly. “You need to start learning how to use your superpowers properly. There’s no way Dad and I can teach you that. Some time with your uncle and aunt is just what you need to get you on track.” So that was that!

pages.heading: The Drive
pages.text: The drive to Aunt Bella’s and Uncle Mark’s the following Saturday was a long one, spent mostly in silence. Mum kept trying to chat, but I couldn’t face it. I just plugged myself into my music and kept my eyes fixed on the scenery as it streamed past us. Finally, the car stopped at our Super relatives’ house. It didn’t look all that Super – it was a normal size, with a normal number of windows and doors, and no sign of any turrets or towers or secret underground lairs. I still didn’t feel enthusiastic about staying there, though. Still, I knew I didn’t really have a choice. So, I took off my headphones, got out of the car and even managed to stick a smile on my face.
pages.imageAlt: A girl in headphones looking out of a car window at pine trees.

pages.heading: Aunt Bella and Uncle Mark
pages.text: Aunt Bella must have heard us arriving, because she bounded out of the house before we’d even rung the doorbell. “It’s so good to see you!” she cried. A huge smile lit up her whole face. She hugged Mum enthusiastically, and then turned to me. “Emily! I’ve heard so much about you. It’s going to be such fun having you stay!” Before I could reply, Aunt Bella enveloped me in a massive hug. Mum and I followed Aunt Bella into the house. She led us through into a large, sunny kitchen, and started clattering about with coffee cups. A thin, dark-haired man was sitting at the table – Uncle Mark, presumably. He smiled and welcomed us kindly too, but he didn’t say much. He seemed to prefer to keep himself to himself. Maybe that’s not surprising, come to think of it. It must be really odd to know what everyone around you is thinking! I expect he could tell I had mixed feelings about this whole thing. Awkward!

pages.heading: Cousin Jake
pages.text: Aunt Bella poured coffee for the grown-ups, and told me to look in the fridge for something I’d like to drink. I found a bottle of raspberry lemonade and poured myself a glass. Just then, I heard loud footsteps running downstairs, fast as a burst of machine-gun fire. A dark-haired boy skidded into the room – my cousin Jake. He looked to be a couple of years younger than me – maybe about thirteen.

pages.heading: A Voice in My Head
pages.text: “Pour me one of those!” said Jake, gesturing to the lemonade. Rude! I thought to myself, but I poured him a glass anyway. “Yes, rude!” came a strange voice. It seemed to be echoing inside my head. I glanced over at Uncle Mark, who smiled slightly. No one else seemed to have heard it. “Jake!” scolded Aunt Bella. “That’s no way to introduce yourself to your cousin. Go back out and come in again properly!” Reluctantly, Jake obeyed her, and then the grown-ups carried on chatting. I felt like I’d had a glimpse of the true Jake, though. He obviously liked to get his own way.

pages.heading: Swingball
pages.text: After coffee, Mum headed back home. It was hard watching her drive off, but Aunt Bella gave me a big hug. At least Aunt Bella’s really nice, I thought. Uncle Mark seems okay too. Not sure about Jake, though. When Mum had gone, Aunt Bella was obviously keen to find something to take my mind off things. “Why don’t you show Emily the garden, Jake?” she said. “You could get the swingball set out.” “OK,” grunted Jake, and he charged through the back door and out into the garden.

pages.heading: The Back Garden
pages.text: The back garden was pretty nice. It was MUCH longer than our garden, with flower beds down each side. “What do you want to do?” I asked Jake. “I’d be up for a game of swingball if you like.” “Huh!” sneered Jake. “Swingball’s for babies! Let’s have a race. First one to the bottom of the garden and back.” I remembered Jake’s superhero name – Rocket Boy. Hmm, no wonder he wants to race, I thought. Something tells me I’m not going to win this one … But I couldn’t think of a reason to refuse, so, “OK,” I said. “You’re on.”
pages.imageAlt: A long back garden with a stone path between bright flower beds.

pages.heading: The Race
pages.text: “Marks, set, go!” shouted Jake. He paused for a second, as if he was revving up internally, and then whoosh! He zoomed down the garden so fast that my eyes couldn’t keep track of him – he was just a long streaming blur. He was back at the start before I’d even managed a couple of metres. “I win, I win!” Jake crowed. “And you lose, Carrot Girl! I’ve heard all about your so-called superpowers. Now you know what real superpowers look like!” Just at that moment, Aunt Bella came out into the garden. She looked completely furious. “Jake!” she shouted. “Apologise to your cousin!”

pages.heading: Splashwoman
pages.text: Jake just smirked and ignored her. Aunt Bella wasn’t having that. She seemed to gather up all her energy, and then she extended one hand. A powerful jet of water shot out, drenching Jake. I almost felt sorry for him, for a moment – he looked so bedraggled. He scowled, apologised grudgingly, and trudged back inside to dry out. “I’m so sorry, Emily,” said Aunt Bella. “Jake can be very insensitive, and he hasn’t really learnt how to handle his superpowers yet.” “He’s not wrong, though,” I said. “My superpowers are a bit rubbish.” “Not at all!” said Aunt Bella warmly. “You’ve been entrusted with your superpowers for a reason, Emily. You just have to get used to them – then you’ll see that you’re just as good as the rest of us.” That was kind of Aunt Bella, but I didn’t really believe her.

pages.heading: The Theme Park
pages.text: The next few days passed slowly. It was summer holiday, so Aunt Bella and Uncle Mark took us on a few trips. We went to the zoo one day, and then to a nearby theme park. This involved a lot of queuing. While we were waiting for the Mega Death Drop ride, Aunt Bella used her Splashwoman superpowers again! The man who was trying to queue-jump couldn’t quite work out where the sudden burst of water came from, but the force of the jet picked him up and delivered him back to the end of the queue. Everyone cheered! Jake looked really embarrassed, though.
pages.imageAlt: A man being swept through the air by a huge jet of water above a theme park queue.

pages.heading: Showing Off
pages.text: On these outings, Jake was reasonably polite to me while his parents were watching. However, when their backs were turned, he always insisted on showing off his super-speed, or mockingly calling me Carrot Girl. By the first weekend, I was beginning to wonder if I’d even get the chance to use my superpowers on this visit. What was the good in coming here to learn how to harness my powers, if I never got a chance to use them?

pages.heading: Party Night
pages.text: That Saturday evening, Uncle Mark and Aunt Bella had to go out to a party. “The pair of you are too old to need a babysitter,” said Aunt Bella. “We won’t be late, anyway. I’m sure you can entertain yourselves for an hour or so without us boring grown-ups! We’ll only be round the corner, so just give us a call if there are any problems.” My heart sank at the thought of a whole evening with just Jake, but what could I do?

pages.heading: A Masterclass
pages.text: The first part of the evening was uneventful. Uncle Mark had left a cold supper out for us in the kitchen, and once we’d eaten that, Jake went off to play computer games by himself – which suited me fine. I lit some scented candles, drew the curtains and then settled down to read. A couple of hours later, just as it was getting properly dark, Jake came down to the living room to find me. “My console’s out of charge,” he said. “I know what we can do instead, though. Why don’t I give you a superpowers masterclass? Watch and learn, Carrot Girl, watch and learn.”
pages.imageAlt: A girl reading in an armchair by candlelight.

pages.heading: Danger!
pages.text: Jake did that weird revving up thing again. Then, before I could even blink, he was off – zooming around the house in a blur of speed. I rolled my eyes. But then I noticed something strange. The skin on my arms was beginning to glow. Pale orange at first, then brighter and brighter. This could only mean one thing – danger! At that moment, Jake whirled back into the living room like a tornado. He knocked over the little table with my candle on it. Then he knocked over a tall lamp, and just at that moment, all the lights went out. The whole house was plunged into darkness – except for a little flicker of light down on the carpet. It was on fire!
pages.imageAlt: A fallen candle setting fire to a carpet.

pages.heading: Dark-Vision
pages.text: My skin was glowing brighter orange than ever, but luckily my dark-vision had kicked in. Jake was standing stock-still, his eyes wide with fear. I had never felt cooler or more certain what to do. I ran to the kitchen for a bowl of water, and before the fire could spread, I quickly put it out. Jake was now gibbering slightly with panic and amazement. Then I unplugged the toppled lamp, and ran to find the electricity fuse box. I flipped the switches, and at once the lights came back on.

pages.heading: How Did You Know?
pages.text: “How … how did you know what to do?” asked Jake, amazed. “Oh, I’ve known for ages what to do if the electricity goes off – and how to put out a small fire,” I said. “For big ones you have to call the fire brigade, but that little fire was nothing I couldn’t handle. You don’t need superpowers to do things like that!” “But how did you react so quickly?” said Jake. “Even I’m not that fast!” “I can sense when bad things are about to happen,” I explained coolly. “My skin grows orange – like a carrot.” “Wow!” said Jake, shaking his head in amazement. “You really are Carrot Girl!”

pages.heading: Carrot Girl Saves the Day
pages.text: Just at that moment, Aunt Bella and Uncle Mark came back. I quickly explained what had happened. “That’s wonderful, Emily!” said Aunt Bella. “Not only did you use your superpowers, but you used your common sense too. Which is more than I can say for you, Jake!” Jake was sent straight up to bed, and grounded for the next three days. I went to bed that night feeling much better about myself. My superpowers did come in useful, I thought. Jake’s speed actually caused the accident, but my early warning system and my night vision saved the day. I kept calm in an emergency, too. Hmm, maybe being Carrot Girl is going to be fun after all!
pages.imageAlt: A smiling girl tucked up in bed.

glossary.pathetic: Weak and not good enough; deserving pity.
glossary.lairs: Hidden places where someone lives or hides.
glossary.clattering: Making a loud, rattling noise with hard things.
glossary.gesturing: Pointing or moving your hand to show what you mean.
glossary.gibbering: Talking fast without making sense, because of fear or shock.
